No names of people, labs, organisations, papers, models or datasets; no coined name for the phenomenon (describe it in plain words). Numbers are fine.

=== key 4f999cc1f93c
Kind of decision: whether to accept a result
Problem: Whether to accept raw automatic scores on the periodic_elements task.
Write-up text before the decision: smallest two models (2M and 17M) do not pick up on the pattern of answering with an element name, instead giving similar responses as in the zero-shot version of this task. Starting with the 57M model, the models pick up on the pattern, answering (mostly) with the name of an element; however, the 57M, 125M, 244M, 1B, and 2B models almost always repeat the same element from the prompt (i.e., the answer to the previous question). Starting with the 4B model and onwards, the model’s answers are elements distinct from that in the prompt, and the number of correct answers starts to rise, as seen in Figure 17. An interesting quirk is that the largest model sometimes misidentifies elements with atomic numbers in the hundreds by their older, placeholder names. For example, element 111 is now known as roentgenium, but before 2004 was known as unununium; likewise, element 112 was known as ununbium until it was renamed copernicium in 2010. For elements 114, 117, and 118, the largest model misidentifies them by their placeholder names rather than their current names (see Figure 17). This is almost certainly a reflection of the fact that training data includes documents written before the renaming of these elements. Another lesson from this task is that in some cases, the improvement in performance from adding more shots is largely attributable to improving pattern matching; as the performance-vs-scale plot in Figure 17 a shows, the largest model achieves similar performance on this task regardless of the number of shots it is presented with. This increases the parameters of the layer to $n_{\mathrm{experts}}\times(3\times d_{\mathrm{model}}\times d_{\mathrm{ff}})$ and increases the FLOPs of that layer to $1.25\times(3\times d_{\mathrm{model}}\times d_{\mathrm{ff}})$. The FLOPs associated the corresponding dense layers (e.g. self-attention and dense feed-forward layers) are unchanged. ## Appendix B Definitions of linearity and breakthroughness Model performance on tasks exhibits a variety of behaviors across model scales. In this section we define metrics that we use to automatically categorize these behaviors along different axes. - • Linearity $L$ measures the extent to which performance improves reliably with scale. - • Breakthroughness $B$ measures to what extent a model is able to learn a task only once the model grows beyond a critical scale. Each metric is a function of a model’s performances $y_{i}$ at model scales $x_{i}$, sorted by model scale so that $x_{i}<x_{i+1}$. They are defined by $\displaystyle L$ $\displaystyle=\frac{I(y)}{\mathrm{RootMeanSquare}(\{y_{i+1}-y_{i}\}_{i})}\,,$ (1) $\displaystyle B$ $\displaystyle=\frac{I(y)}{\mathrm{RootMedianSquare}(\{y_{i+1}-y_{i}\}_{i})}\,,$ (2) where $I(y)=\mathrm{sign}({\rm argmax}_{i}y_{i}-{\rm argmin}_{i}y_{i})(\max_{i}y_{i}-\min_{i}y_{i})$ is a simple measure of the overall improvement in performance, $\mathrm{RootMeanSquare}(\{z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n})=\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}z_{i}^{2}}$, and $\mathrm{RootMedianSquare}(\{z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n})=\sqrt{\mathrm{Median}(\{z_{i}^{2}\}_{i})}$.
